sharedText: I have somewhat more to say unto thee
reason: 'I have somewhat more to say unto thee than what I said unto thy brother.' 'I have somewhat to say unto thee' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Kings 2:14 and Luke 7:40, and Luke 7:40 is uncomfortably apt: Jesus says it to Simon the Pharisee in the one Gospel scene where a man is rebuked over his attitude to a woman who was a sinner, and what follows is a parable about which of two debtors loves more. Alma 39:1 introduces a rebuke over a harlot. The row is declined because the phrase is ordinary English rather than a KJV signature — Alma has already used it at 37:38 of a compass, where no such setting is available, and the addition of 'more' and the comparison to the brother are the sentence's real work. Recorded because a reader who knows Luke 7 will feel the pull and should be told the catalogue felt it too.

sharedText: boasting in thy strength, and thy wisdom
reason: The prohibition of boasting in wisdom and in strength is adjudicated one chapter earlier, at Alma 38:11, where Alma gives it to Shiblon as a caution ('see that ye do not boast in your own wisdom, nor of your much strength') and where the case for Jeremiah 9:23 — the KJV's one prohibition pairing those two boasts in that order — is argued with its counter-evidence. Alma 39:2 is the same pair in reverse order and in the indicative, as a charge rather than a warning: what the obedient son was told to avoid is what the disobedient one is convicted of. The pairing is registered in the recurrence list at Alma 38:11. See Alma 38:11.

sharedText: she did steal away the hearts of many
reason: 'Yea, she did steal away the hearts of many.' 'Stole the hearts' is a KJV singleton, at 2 Samuel 15:6, of Absalom stealing the hearts of the men of Israel, and the Book of Mormon uses the figure repeatedly. Its adjudication in this book is at Alma 17:29, with Alma 47:30 and Mosiah 27:9 elsewhere in the corpus; by Alma 39 the heart-stealing formula is the book's own — it recurs three more times inside this chapter alone (39:11, 39:12, 39:13, always of leading hearts away), which is the signature of an internal formula rather than a fresh borrowing (ADJUDICATING §4). See Alma 17:29.

sharedText: deny the Holy Ghost when it once hath had place in you
reason: The apostasy passage a reader will reach for first, and rightly — Hebrews 6:4-6's 'once enlightened … made partakers of the Holy Ghost … if they shall fall away, to renew them again unto repentance' is the New Testament's fullest statement of a sin committed after the Spirit has been received. Both 'once enlightened' and 'partakers of the Holy Ghost' are KJV singletons in that passage. It is adjudicated in this book at Alma 24:30, where the Book of Mormon reproduces 'once enlightened' itself and where the composite runs on to 2 Peter 2:20-21. Alma 39:6 has the idea without any of that verse's words, and it has instead the distinct argument of Hebrews 10:26-29 — wilfulness after knowledge, and a remedy withdrawn — which is where the link at this verse is filed. See Alma 24:30 and the Hebrews 10:26 row at this verse.

'I would to God that ye had not been guilty of so great a crime.' The machine ranks this first in the verse and the temptation is stronger than the run alone, because Alma 36 has just quarried Acts 26 heavily — Acts 26:14 stands behind Alma 36:7 — so Paul before Agrippa is genuinely in the neighbourhood. But 'I would to God' occurs in two KJV verses (Acts 26:29 and 1 Corinthians 4:8) and is a dead optative idiom in seventeenth-century English rather than a citation; neither KJV context has anything to do with a father's grief over a son's crime. The verse's memorable phrase, 'to harrow up your soul', is not biblical at all: 'harrow' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 39:10, of a unicorn dragging a harrow through a valley. It is the Book of Mormon's own, established at Alma 36:12.

sharedText: him that surely shall come, to take away the sins of the world
reason: 'It is him that surely shall come, to take away the sins of the world.' John 1:29's 'the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world' is adjudicated in this book at Alma 7:14, at certain, where the Book of Mormon reproduces the clause verbatim but for the plural 'sins' — the same plural that appears here. Alma 39:15 has the clause without the Lamb, converted from a present participle to a future ('shall come, to take away'), which is the change the chapter's argument about a Christ eighty years off requires. The verse's own link is to Luke 1:77, for the second half of the sentence. See Alma 7:14.
